Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
reference_answer: No. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk under this ground only where both conditions are cumulatively met: (a) it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, which includes the Medical Devices Regulation, and (b) that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market. MDR Class I devices that are non-sterile, non-measuring and not reusable surgical instruments follow the internal-control (self-assessment) procedure, with no notified body involved. Since condition (b) is not satisfied, the Article 6(1) test fails, so the AI safety component is not automatically high-risk on this basis.

question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), can the same AI system be subject both to the Act's "high-risk AI system" obligations and to the transparency obligations sometimes described informally as "limited risk"? Explain briefly.
criteria: Yes
Article 50(6): Article 50(1)-(4) transparency duties do not affect Chapter III high-risk obligations
Obligations are cumulative, not mutually exclusive
reference_answer: Yes. Article 50(6) expressly states that the transparency obligations in Article 50(1) to (4) do not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III for high-risk AI systems, and are without prejudice to other transparency obligations in Union or national law. High-risk classification depends on the system's intended purpose under Article 6/Annex III, while Article 50 duties attach whenever a system interacts with people, generates synthetic content, or performs emotion recognition/biometric categorisation, regardless of risk tier. The two regimes are therefore cumulative: a high-risk system that also does these things must satisfy both sets of obligations simultaneously, and compliance with one does not substitute for the other.

question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a toy qualify as a high-risk AI system, and if so under what conditions?
criteria: Yes
Condition: AI system is a toy or safety component of a toy covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I harmonisation legislation)
Condition: that toy is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Directive
Both conditions cumulative (Article 6(1))
reference_answer: Yes. Article 6(1) provides a route to high-risk classification outside Annex III: an AI system is high-risk if it is itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Annex I includes Directive 2009/48/EC on toy safety. So an AI-enabled toy, or an AI system that is a safety component of a toy, qualifies as high-risk only if both conditions are met cumulatively: it falls within the Toy Safety Directive's scope, and the Directive requires third-party (not merely self-) conformity assessment for that toy. If either condition fails, the toy AI system is not high-risk under Article 6(1).

question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
criteria: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
reference_answer: Yes. Under Article 6(1), an AI system intended as a safety component of a lift is high-risk only where two cumulative conditions are met: the lift is a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that legislation requires the lift to undergo third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service. Lifts fall under such Annex I legislation (Directive 2014/33/EU). If third-party conformity assessment is mandated, the safety-component AI system is high-risk; if only self-assessment applies, this ground is not satisfied, though another ground could still apply.

question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), are AI systems intended for emotion recognition from biometric data always prohibited? If not, in which contexts are they prohibited, what exception applies, and how are they classified when not prohibited?
criteria: No
Prohibited context: inferring emotions of natural persons in workplace and education institutions (Article 5(1)(f))
Exception: use intended for medical or safety reasons
When not prohibited, classified as high-risk under Annex III (emotion recognition/biometrics category)
reference_answer: No, emotion-recognition AI systems are not categorically prohibited. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service, or using such systems to infer the emotions of a natural person specifically in the areas of the workplace and education institutions. An exception applies where the system is intended to be put into service or placed on the market for medical or safety reasons, so the prohibition does not apply even in those two settings. Outside the prohibited contexts, and under the medical/safety exception, emotion-recognition systems are not banned but are instead classified as high-risk AI systems under Annex III (biometrics category, point 1(c)), subjecting them to the Chapter III high-risk obligations.

question: I generated audio with AI for my artistic work (sole purpose). Do I need to provide some marking of its artificial nature? I feel that would compromise the enjoyment of the work.
criteria: Yes, disclosure still required
No need for marking that hampers enjoyment
Must disclose existence of AI-generated content in appropriate/unobtrusive manner
reference_answer: Yes, but in reduced form. Since this is a deep fake within an evidently artistic work, Article 50(4) does not remove the transparency obligation entirely—it limits it. You are not required to mark the audio in a way that hampers the display or enjoyment of the work, so a prominent or intrusive label is not necessary. However, you must still disclose, in some appropriate and unobtrusive manner, that the audio content was artificially generated or manipulated. The existence of AI generation must be disclosed; only the manner of disclosure is relaxed to preserve the work's enjoyment.

question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
criteria: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
reference_answer: Under Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, "risk" is defined as the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.

question: For AI systems that fit within the use cases listed in Annex III but are considered non-high-risk by the provider, do they need to be registered in the EU database?
criteria: Yes
Registration required under Article 49(2)
Registered in EU database referred to in Article 71
reference_answer: Yes. Even where a provider concludes under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk, Article 49(2) still requires that provider, or its authorised representative, to register itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before placing it on the market or putting it into service. This obligation is distinct from the Article 49(1) duty covering actually high-risk systems, but applies for the same reason: the system falls within an Annex III use case, so its non-high-risk classification must remain visible and traceable rather than exempting it from registration entirely.

question: Do I need informed consent to test a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside a regulatory sandbox?
criteria: Yes

Consent must be freely given and informed, obtained prior to participation, covering nature/objectives/inconveniences, conditions and duration, rights to refuse/withdraw without detriment or justification, reversal/disregard arrangements, and the unique ID plus provider contact details
Consent must be dated, documented, and a copy given to the subject or their legal representative
reference_answer: Yes. Under Article 61, testing a high-risk AI system in real world conditions requires freely-given, informed consent from each testing subject, obtained before their participation begins. Subjects must first receive concise, clear and understandable information covering the nature, objectives and possible inconveniences of the test, its conditions and expected duration, their right to refuse or withdraw at any time without detriment or justification, the arrangements for requesting reversal or disregarding of the system's outputs, and the test's unique identification number and the provider's contact details. The consent must be dated and documented, with a copy given to the subject or their legal representative.

question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
criteria: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
reference_answer: Both obligations apply; they are not alternatives. Under Article 20(1), once a provider considers or has reason to consider its high-risk AI system non-compliant, it must immediately take the necessary corrective action — bring the system into conformity, withdraw, disable, or recall it — and inform distributors and, where applicable, deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Separately, under Article 20(2), once the provider becomes aware the system presents a risk within Article 79(1), it must itself immediately investigate the causes, collaborating with the reporting deployer where applicable, and then inform the competent market surveillance authority (and notified body, where relevant) of the non-compliance and any corrective action taken. The investigation duty rests with the provider, not the market surveillance authority, which is only informed afterward.

question: What is Article 50(4) about?
criteria: Deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating image, audio or video constituting a deep fake must disclose the content is artificially generated or manipulated
Exception where use is authorised by law to detect/prevent/investigate/prosecute criminal offences
For evidently artistic/creative/satirical/fictional/analogous works, obligation limited to disclosing existence of such content without hampering enjoyment/display

Separate rule: deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose artificial generation, with exceptions for law-enforcement authorisation or human review/editorial responsibility
reference_answer: Article 50(4) sets deployer-side transparency obligations for synthetic content. Deployers of an AI system generating or manipulating image, audio or video content that constitutes a deep fake must disclose that it is artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. For evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, this is limited to disclosing the existence of such content in a way that does not hamper its display or enjoyment. Separately, deployers of AI generating or manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose its artificial origin, unless the same law-enforcement exception applies or the content underwent human review or editorial control with an identifiable person or entity holding editorial responsibility.

question: Is an AI system high-risk if it is used in a product that: is not listed in Annex I; use case not listed in Annex III; internally uses general purpose AI model with systemic risk due to high impact capabilities?
criteria: No
Article 6(1) not met: not an Annex I product/safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment
Article 6(2) not met: use case not listed in Annex III
Internal use of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk is not an Article 6 criterion
reference_answer: No. Under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk only if it satisfies paragraph 1 (it is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment) or paragraph 2 (its use case is listed in Annex III). Neither condition is met here, since the product falls outside Annex I and the use case falls outside Annex III. The system's internal use of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk is not a criterion under Article 6; such models are instead subject to their own separate obligations under Articles 51-56.

question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
criteria: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
reference_answer: The model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) of the AI Act expressly obliges distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the Section 2 requirements. The "where applicable" qualifier acknowledges that a high-risk AI system may be pure software, but it is often embedded in or supplied with hardware, or distributed on physical media, so storage and transport can be relevant. Where no physical storage or transport occurs, the obligation simply has no practical content, but it still exists as a distributor duty under Article 24.

question:
Given an AI system that is high-risk according to Annex III: if it is repurposed to a use case not in Annex III (nor Annex I), then:
- the repurposed AI system is still high-risk due to reversibility of training into the original system
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk but it must be reported in the EU database
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database
criteria: No longer high-risk (third option)
High-risk status attaches to intended purpose/use case under Article 6(2)/Annex III, not to the system or its training as such
New use case outside Annex III and Annex I means neither limb of Article 6 is satisfied
No registration/EU database obligation (Article 49/Article 71) since system is not high-risk
reference_answer: The repurposed system is no longer high-risk, and there is no need to report it in the EU database. Under Article 6(2), high-risk classification attaches to the AI system by reference to Annex III use cases (or, under Article 6(1), Annex I safety-component coverage) — i.e., to its intended purpose, not to the underlying model or its training. Reversibility of training into the original system is irrelevant. Once the provider redirects the system to a use case outside both Annex III and Annex I, neither limb of Article 6 is met, so the system exits the high-risk category entirely. Since it is not high-risk, the registration duty under Article 49 and the EU database under Article 71 do not apply.

question: We have a phone system where the caller can press 1 if they consent to the call being recorded, 2 if they do not. We wish to replace this with an NLP system that understands a voice reply like "Yes", "Sure", "Please no", etc. Would such a system be considered high-risk? It's for our clinic.
criteria: No
Not biometric categorisation or emotion recognition under Annex III(1)(b)-(c), since the system parses semantic content (yes/no), not emotional or protected-attribute inference
Not essential healthcare services under Annex III(5)(a), since consent capture for call recording is not an eligibility evaluation for benefits/services
reference_answer: No, this system would not be high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III(1)(b)-(c) covers AI used for biometric categorisation or emotion recognition, but this system merely interprets the literal semantic content of a spoken reply (yes/no) to determine consent, not any emotional or sensitive/protected attribute inferred from voice, so it falls outside that category. It also does not fall under Annex III(5)(a), since that provision concerns evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare, not capturing consent to call recording. Since no Annex III area applies, the system is not high-risk, regardless of the clinic context.

question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
criteria: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
reference_answer: The AI Act does not prohibit or classify drones as such as high-risk; under Article 6, classification depends on the AI system's intended use, not the device carrying it. Using a drone's AI to identify who is present in town is remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), since it identifies individuals rather than merely verifying a single claimed identity (the verification exclusion doesn't apply). A toy drone is treated no differently — being a toy does not exempt the system, so this same use remains high-risk. A toy drone used for another application is high-risk only if that application matches an Annex III use case, or is a safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1).

question: Does the EU AI Act establish a "proportionality of need" requirement according to which very powerful but environmentally impactful models (e.g. LLMs) should not be used for simple tasks (e.g. sentiment recognition) when a simpler and performant model is available (e.g. BERT)? If yes, cite which Article or Annex mentions this.
criteria: No
No provision conditions use of a capable model on unavailability of a simpler/less resource-intensive alternative for the same task
Obligations are risk- and capability-based (e.g. Article 6, Annex III, Article 51), not tied to model right-sizing or environmental impact
reference_answer: No. The AI Act does not establish a "proportionality of need" or model-right-sizing requirement obliging providers or deployers to use a simpler, less environmentally impactful model (e.g. BERT) instead of a more powerful one (e.g. an LLM) when performing a simple task like sentiment recognition. Its obligations are structured around risk classification (Article 6, Annex III) and, for general-purpose AI models, capability thresholds (Article 51), plus transparency duties such as Article 50 - none of which condition lawful use of a high-capacity model on the unavailability of a lighter alternative. No Article or Annex imposes such a substitution or minimal-sufficiency principle, so none can be cited.

question: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?
criteria: No
Article 9 only establishes the risk management system for high-risk AI systems, not a five-tier harm classification

Four steps: identify/analyze risks (9(2)(a)); estimate/evaluate risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse (9(2)(b)); evaluate risks from post-market monitoring data (9(2)(c)); adopt targeted risk management measures (9(2)(d))
The prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk/systemic-risk tiering comes from elsewhere in the Regulation (e.g. Articles 5, 6, 50, 51), not Article 9
reference_answer: No. Article 9 does not list five categories of harm mapped to risk tiers; it solely requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish, implement, document and maintain a continuous, iterative risk management system throughout the system's lifecycle. That system comprises four steps: identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights; estimation and evaluation of risks arising from intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluation of further risks identified via post-market monitoring data; and adoption of targeted risk management measures addressing the risks found. The Act's prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk/systemic-risk architecture instead derives from other provisions, such as Articles 5, 6, 50 and 51.

question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
criteria: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
reference_answer: No. Under Article 26(1), deployers must use a high-risk AI system in accordance with its instructions for use; deploying it for a purpose outside that intended use breaches this obligation, regardless of whether the new use, viewed in isolation, would independently qualify as high-risk under Annex III. The system's high-risk classification attaches to it as placed on the market, so a deployer cannot unilaterally reassess risk use-by-use to sidestep Article 26. Logging duties are unaffected: under Article 26(6), deployers must still keep the automatically generated logs, to the extent under their control, for at least six months, irrespective of which use generated them.

question: Is an AI that transcribes doctor-patient conversations prohibited? Or is it high-risk as per the use cases of Annex III of the AI Act?
criteria: No, not a prohibited practice under Article 5
No, not high-risk under Annex III
Reason: narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), point (a)
reference_answer: No to both. Transcribing doctor-patient conversations is not among the prohibited practices listed in Article 5. It also does not qualify as high-risk under Annex III: even if used in a context otherwise touching an Annex III area, transcription is a narrow procedural task within the meaning of Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), so the derogation removes it from high-risk classification. This holds because the system does not materially influence the outcome of any healthcare decision and does not perform profiling of natural persons, which would otherwise override the derogation.

question: As a deployer, do I need to keep logs if I use a powerful LLM (surpassing the FLOPs threshold) for estimating whether customer payment confirmations are received via email?
criteria: No
Article 26(6) logging duty applies only to deployers of high-risk AI systems
This use case is not a high-risk use case listed in Annex III
FLOPs threshold concerns GPAI systemic-risk classification under Article 51, a separate regime irrelevant to Annex III high-risk classification
reference_answer: No. The Article 26(6) log-keeping duty applies only to deployers of high-risk AI systems, i.e. systems falling within an Annex III use case (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or justice/democracy). Estimating whether customer payment confirmation emails were received is an ordinary administrative function that does not correspond to any Annex III area, so the system is not high-risk. The fact that the underlying LLM surpasses the FLOPs threshold is irrelevant here: that threshold governs classification of a general-purpose AI model as posing systemic risk under Article 51, a distinct regime from the Article 6/Annex III high-risk classification of AI systems. No Article 26(6) obligation therefore arises.

question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
criteria: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
reference_answer: Yes. AI software that helps clinicians decide on the best treatment falls under Article 6(2), which deems high-risk the AI systems listed in Annex III. Annex III covers AI systems intended to be used for triage or to make or materially influence decisions on access to and enjoyment of essential public and private services, including healthcare provision. Since treatment-decision support materially influences a healthcare outcome affecting a natural person, it is classified as high-risk, unless one of the narrow-task carve-outs in Article 6(3) applies.

question: Do Annex I, Annex II, and Annex III all have to deal with high-risk AI classifications? If not, which doesn't/do not, and what is/are it/they about?
criteria: No
Annex II is the one that does not - it lists criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), a prohibited-practices provision, not high-risk classification
Annex I and Annex III both relate to high-risk classification - Annex I (Union harmonisation legislation) feeds Article 6(1), Annex III (use-case areas) is referred to in Article 6(2)
reference_answer: No. Annex I and Annex III both concern high-risk classification, while Annex II does not. Annex I lists Union harmonisation legislation (e.g. machinery, toys, medical devices, civil aviation, motor vehicles) covering products that become high-risk under Article 6(1) when an AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, such a product subject to third-party conformity assessment. Annex III lists the specific high-risk use-case areas (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, etc.) referred to in Article 6(2). Annex II instead lists criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), which defines the law-enforcement exception to the prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces - a prohibited-practices matter, not high-risk classification.

question: Is irregular migration a topic considered in the AI Act? If so, to what risk category does it belong?
criteria: Yes
Migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7)
High-risk
reference_answer: Yes. Annex III, point 7(b) expressly lists AI systems used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, to assess a risk—including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk—posed by a natural person who intends to enter or has entered a Member State's territory. These systems fall within the "migration, asylum and border control management" area of Annex III and are therefore classified as high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2), subject to the Regulation's applicable requirements.

question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
criteria: Date of release - Yes
Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No
reference_answer: Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII, a GPAI provider must give downstream AI system providers, at minimum: the date of release (yes); the architecture and number of parameters (yes); how the model interacts with, or can be used to interact with, hardware or software where applicable (yes); and the licence applicable to the model (yes). Samples of outlier training data are not required (no), since Annex XII only obliges disclosure of the type and provenance of training, testing and validation data and the curation methods applied, not actual data samples.

question: Who, if at all, needs to establish the post-market monitoring system for a high-risk AI system? Provider/deployer/AI office? Is it possible that the monitoring system may need to also include info on interaction with other AI systems than the high-risk one in consideration?
criteria: Provider
Not deployer or AI Office
Yes — must include analysis of interaction with other AI systems where relevant
reference_answer: Under Article 72(1), the provider of the high-risk AI system — not the deployer or the AI Office — must establish and document the post-market monitoring system, proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and risks involved, though deployers (and other sources) may supply data feeding into it. Per Article 72(2), the system must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse performance data throughout the system's lifetime to evaluate continuous compliance. Where relevant, it must also include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems, so its scope is not limited to the high-risk system in isolation, subject to an exclusion for sensitive operational data of law-enforcement deployers.

question: What is an "area" and what is a "use case" for high-risk as per Article 6(2)? How many areas exist?
criteria: Area = broad Annex III numbered heading/policy domain
Use case = specific application listed within an area (lettered sub-point)
8 areas exist
reference_answer: Article 6(2) provides that AI systems listed in Annex III are considered high-risk. Annex III is organised into broad "areas" — numbered headings covering policy domains of societal importance, such as biometrics, education, employment, and law enforcement. Within each area, "use cases" are the specific, more granular applications set out in the lettered sub-points, describing the concrete AI deployment scenarios that trigger high-risk classification. So an area is a policy field, while a use case is a particular application within that field. Annex III currently contains eight such areas.

question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
criteria: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
reference_answer: Annex III lists eight high-risk areas: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision making is not itself a separate listed area. It only appears within the essential-services area, covering AI used to evaluate eligibility for public assistance benefits and services including healthcare, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems.

question: What does Annex VII point 5.1 say? Try to get the substance right. Do not get confused with other material, like 5.1 in Annex III or Article 7, which is about something else entirely.
criteria: Purpose of surveillance is to ensure the provider duly complies with the terms and conditions of the approved quality management system
reference_answer: Annex VII point 5.1 states that the purpose of the surveillance carried out by the notified body referred to in point 3 is to make sure that the provider duly complies with the terms and conditions of the approved quality management system. This is part of the ongoing surveillance phase of the Annex VII conformity assessment procedure (based on quality management system plus technical documentation assessment), distinct from unrelated provisions elsewhere in the Regulation, such as Annex III point 5.1 or Article 7.

question: Do providers of GPAI systems, even if not with systemic risk, have an obligation to extensively shield their models from adversarial attacks? What about specifically for adversarial images? What about specifically for prompt injection?
criteria: No
Applies only to GPAI models with systemic risk, under Article 55(1)(a)
Adversarial images not separately addressed - only general adversarial-testing duty
Prompt injection not separately addressed - not mentioned in Article 55
reference_answer: No. The obligation to shield models from adversarial attacks does not apply to providers of general-purpose AI models generally; under Article 55(1)(a), it falls only on providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, who must perform model evaluation using standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks. Article 55(1)(a) does not single out adversarial images as a distinct category, referring only generically to adversarial testing. Prompt injection is likewise not separately addressed anywhere in Article 55, so no specific obligation regarding it exists, regardless of systemic-risk status.

question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
criteria: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
reference_answer: No. Article 6(3) is not a sliding scale to an intermediate "moderate risk" tier - an Annex III system either stays high-risk or is exempted, and guardrails alone do not exempt it. Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself falls within one of four conditions: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting deviations from prior human decisions without replacing that assessment, or a preparatory task. Changing the system's capabilities and intended use can reclassify it, but only if the redefined purpose satisfies one of these conditions. This exemption never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons.

question: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?
criteria: Yes, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency
Authorisation must be requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours
If refused: use stopped immediately, all data/results/outputs discarded and deleted
reference_answer: Yes. Article 5(3) allows law enforcement to commence use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces without prior authorisation only in a duly justified situation of urgency. Authorisation from the competent judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding must nonetheless be requested without undue delay, and at the latest within 24 hours. If that authorisation is subsequently rejected, the use must be stopped with immediate effect, and all data, results and outputs generated from that use must be immediately discarded and deleted.

question: Consider a private contractor of the municipality that runs a city's emergency-call triage platform. The contractor plans to use an AI tool to prioritize police response decisions. Before going live with the system, does this contractor need to look into fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA)? Is this because of this scenario belonging to Annex III 5(b) or 5(c)? What about private contractors offering other public services concerning Annex III but NOT specifically 5(b) or 5(c)?
criteria: Yes, FRIA required
No — trigger is being a "private entity providing public services" under Article 27(1), not Annex III 5(b)/(c)
5(b)/(c) is a separate, additional limb pulling in deployers of those specific systems even when not providing public services
Other private contractors offering public services outside 5(b)/(c) remain covered via the general public-service limb, for every Annex III area except point 2
reference_answer: Yes. Article 27(1) requires the contractor to perform a FRIA before deploying the system, but the trigger is that it is a private entity providing public services — the general limb of Article 27(1) — not that the use case falls under Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c). Those points instead form a separate, additional limb of Article 27(1), catching deployers of those specific systems even when they are not public-service providers at all. Private contractors delivering other public services within Annex III's scope, but outside 5(b)/(c), are equally caught by the general public-service trigger, which applies to every Annex III high-risk area except point 2 (critical infrastructure).

question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
criteria: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
reference_answer: Yes, this use is permitted; the AI Act does not prohibit deep-fake images for teaching, it only imposes transparency duties. Because the images are a deep fake, Article 50(4) requires the deployer to disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. Such evidently educational, illustrative material can be treated as "analogous" to an artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work, so the lighter regime applies: disclosure need only indicate the existence of the generated content, in a manner that does not hamper its display or enjoyment. This differs from the law-enforcement exception, which is a full exemption from disclosure rather than a lightened requirement, and does not apply to this scenario.

question: If a high-risk AI system was already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, does the AI Act fully apply to it? What about general purpose AI systems?
criteria: No, does not fully apply
Applies only if system undergoes significant changes in design as from 2 August 2026
High-risk systems for public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless
GPAI models placed on market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027
reference_answer: No. Under Article 111(2), the Act does not automatically apply in full to high-risk AI systems already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026; it applies to their operators only if those systems undergo significant changes to their design as from that date. In any case, providers and deployers of high-risk systems intended for use by public authorities must achieve compliance by 2 August 2030. For general-purpose AI models, Article 111(3) sets a separate rule: providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply with the Regulation's obligations by 2 August 2027.

question: What is Annex X about? What is it used for?
criteria: Annex X lists Union legislative acts on large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice (e.g. SIS, VIS, Eurodac, EES, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN, interoperability regulations)
Used in conjunction with Article 111 to set transitional/compliance deadlines for AI systems that are components of these large-scale IT systems
reference_answer: Annex X lists the Union legislative acts establishing and governing large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice: the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN, and the interoperability Regulations (EU) 2019/817 and 2019/818. It is used together with Article 111 to identify AI systems that are components of, or used in operating, these large-scale IT systems, and to fix the specific transitional deadlines by which such systems must be brought into compliance with the Regulation, rather than the general timelines otherwise applying.

question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
criteria: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
reference_answer: No. Annex III.6 confines the law-enforcement high-risk category to AI systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities, covering functions such as assessing risk of offending, evaluating reliability of evidence, or profiling in the course of detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. A supermarket's internal tool flagging cart/checkout anomalies for optional bag checks by store staff is operated by a private retailer, not by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority. The resemblance to investigative or evaluative activity and the possibility of detrimental treatment do not bring it within Annex III.6 absent that law-enforcement-authority nexus.

question: We are a private educational institution intending to deploy an AI tool that analyses students' prior grades and learning outcomes to recommend whether they should follow the standard or accelerated honours track going forward. We remark that a student who receives the "standard" recommendation is *not* barred from choosing accelerated, the system merely provides a suggestion. Are there reasons to believe the system might be high-risk? What articles/annex and specific points, if any, concern this use case?
criteria: Yes
Annex III point 3(c) - assessing appropriate level of education a person will receive/access
Article 6(3) derogation for narrow/preparatory/non-influencing tasks would otherwise apply given the non-binding recommendation
Article 6(3) final subparagraph - Annex III systems are always high-risk if they profile natural persons, overriding the derogation
reference_answer: Yes, there is a solid basis to treat this as high-risk. It falls under Annex III point 3(c), covering AI systems used to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or access within educational institutions, which is exactly what a standard/accelerated track recommendation does. The non-binding nature would normally support Article 6(3)'s derogation, since a mere suggestion that doesn't bar the accelerated option could be seen as a narrow, preparatory, or non-decisive task not materially influencing the outcome. However, Article 6(3)'s final subparagraph overrides this: an Annex III system is always high-risk if it profiles natural persons, and analysing individual grades and learning outcomes to generate a personalised track recommendation is likely to constitute such profiling, so the derogation does not apply.

question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
criteria: No
AI Act Section 2 requirements incorporated into existing Machinery Regulation conformity assessment, not a separate AI Act procedure (Article 43(3))
No EU database registration, since Article 71 applies only to Annex III high-risk systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related ones
reference_answer: No separate, dedicated AI Act conformity assessment is required. The robot is a product covered by the Machinery Regulation (Annex I), and the AI module is its safety component, making it high-risk under Article 6(1). Under Article 43(3), the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure already required under the Machinery Regulation, with the AI Act's Chapter III Section 2 requirements incorporated into and assessed as part of that same procedure, since the notified body is entitled to verify them there. No EU database registration is required either, as the Article 71 registration obligation applies only to high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, not to Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related high-risk systems like this one.

question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
criteria: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
reference_answer: No. Under Article 43(3), for high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by that sectoral legislation, but the Chapter III Section 2 requirements still apply to the system and form part of that very assessment. Opting out of third-party assessment under the sectoral act is permitted only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards, or common specifications under Article 41, covering all the Section 2 requirements, not merely the sectoral ones. So the opt-out changes who performs the assessment, not whether Section 2's substantive requirements must be satisfied.

question: A private contractor runs a region's gas supply service on behalf of the local government. It licenses an AI system from a vendor, fine-tunes it on local data, and then puts it into service under its own brand. To learn about correct applicable classifications of the system and the contractor, what material of the AI Act should I read? Does fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) applies?
criteria: Annex III, point 2 together with Article 6(2) — system classified high-risk as a safety component in gas supply (critical infrastructure)
Article 25(1)(a) — contractor deemed the provider by putting its own name/trademark on the system already placed on the market or put into service
No
FRIA (Article 27) is a deployer obligation; having been reclassified as provider under Article 25(1)(a), the contractor is not acting as deployer of this system
reference_answer: Read Article 6(2) together with Annex III, point 2: AI systems used as safety components in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, including the supply of gas, are high-risk. For the contractor's status, read Article 25(1)(a): by putting the licensed, fine-tuned system into service under its own name or trademark, the contractor is deemed the provider and takes on the Article 16 provider obligations, while the original vendor ceases to be considered the provider for that system. No, FRIA does not apply to the contractor: the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment is a deployer obligation, and here the contractor has been reclassified as provider rather than deployer.
